#Make dummy columns for the categorical values and drop the original columns at the same time
#Make sure to do this in another copy of the data so that you have a backup
dfdum = df.copy()

dfdum = pd.concat([dfdum.drop('workclass', axis=1),
                   pd.get_dummies(dfdum['workclass'], dtype=int, prefix='work')], axis=1)
dfdum = pd.concat([dfdum.drop('education', axis=1),
                   pd.get_dummies(dfdum['education'], dtype=int, prefix='education')], axis=1)
dfdum = pd.concat([dfdum.drop('marital.status', axis=1),
                   pd.get_dummies(dfdum['marital.status'], dtype=int, prefix='marital_status')], axis=1)
dfdum = pd.concat([dfdum.drop('occupation', axis=1),
                   pd.get_dummies(dfdum['occupation'], dtype=int, prefix='occupation')], axis=1)
dfdum = pd.concat([dfdum.drop('relationship', axis=1),
                   pd.get_dummies(dfdum['relationship'], dtype=int, prefix='relationship')], axis=1)
dfdum = pd.concat([dfdum.drop('race', axis=1),
                   pd.get_dummies(dfdum['race'], dtype=int, prefix='race')], axis=1)
dfdum = pd.concat([dfdum.drop('sex', axis=1),
                   pd.get_dummies(dfdum['sex'], dtype=int, prefix='sex')], axis=1)

#Seperate the top 5 countries by frequency and the rest will be combined into another column named others
top5_countries = dfdum['native.country'].value_counts().nlargest(5).index
dfdum['native.country_reduced'] = dfdum['native.country'].where(dfdum['native.country'].isin(top5_countries),'Other_countries')
dfdum = pd.concat([dfdum.drop('native.country', axis=1),
                   pd.get_dummies(dfdum['native.country_reduced']
                                  ,prefix='country',dtype=int)],axis=1)
dfdum = dfdum.drop('native.country_reduced', axis=1)

I used a code to find the VIF that are more than 5 and dropped them

In [7]:
# Separate features and target
X = dfdum.drop(['income','high_income'], axis=1)  # replace 'income' with your target column
y = dfdum['high_income']

# Function to calculate VIF
def calculate_vif(X):
    vif_data = pd.DataFrame()
    vif_data['Feature'] = X.columns
    vif_data['VIF'] = [variance_inflation_factor(X.values, i) for i in range(X.shape[1])]
    return vif_data

# Iteratively drop features with VIF > 5
max_vif = 5
while True:
    vif_df = calculate_vif(X)
    max_vif_value = vif_df['VIF'].max()
    if max_vif_value <= max_vif:
        break
    drop_feature = vif_df.sort_values('VIF', ascending=False)['Feature'].iloc[0]
    print(f"Dropping {drop_feature} with VIF = {max_vif_value:.2f}")
    X = X.drop(columns=[drop_feature])

#Use lpm as the data is binary, linear regression would think that the r squared is low since the values are always low
#LPM will be the compatible model so we will be using that

print("FITTING LINEAR PROBABILITY MODEL (LPM) USING OLS:")
print("-" * 50)

# Add constant term for intercept (required by statsmodels)
X_train_const = sm.add_constant(X_train)
X_test_const = sm.add_constant(X_test)

# Fit the Linear Probability Model using OLS
lpm_model = sm.OLS(y_train, X_train_const)
lpm_results = lpm_model.fit()

print(f"\nMODEL FITTING COMPLETE:")
print(f"- Estimation method: Ordinary Least Squares (OLS)")
print(f"- Number of observations: {lpm_results.nobs}")
print(f"- Number of parameters: {len(lpm_results.params)}")
print(f"- Degrees of freedom: {lpm_results.df_resid}")

# Calculate all metrics
def calculate_metrics(y_true, y_pred):
    accuracy = accuracy_score(y_true, y_pred)
    precision = precision_score(y_true, y_pred)
    recall = recall_score(y_true, y_pred)
    f1 = f1_score(y_true, y_pred)
    
    # Calculate specificity manually
    cm = confusion_matrix(y_true, y_pred)
    tn, fp, fn, tp = cm.ravel()
    specificity = tn / (tn + fp) if (tn + fp) > 0 else 0
    
    return {
        'accuracy': accuracy,
        'precision': precision,
        'recall': recall,
        'specificity': specificity,
        'f1': f1
    }

train_metrics = calculate_metrics(y_train, y_pred_binary_train)
test_metrics = calculate_metrics(y_test, y_pred_binary_test)

        X_clean = X_clean.drop(columns=[cols[0]])  

# Then fit GLM
import statsmodels.api as sm
X_sm = sm.add_constant(X_clean)  
glm_binom = sm.GLM(y, X_sm, family=sm.families.Binomial())
glm_result = glm_binom.fit()
# Exclude intercept
glm_coefs = glm_result.params.drop('const')

# Keep features with |coef| <= 0.5
selected_features = glm_coefs[glm_coefs.abs() <= 0.5].index.tolist()

# Make a new X with only these valid features
X_valid = X_sm[selected_features]  
X_valid = sm.add_constant(X_valid)  

print("Valid features for GLM after filtering by coefficient magnitude:")
print(X_valid.columns)

print(glm_result.summary())

print("=" * 60)

# Fit LPM using sklearn LinearRegression
lpm_model = LinearRegression()
lpm_model.fit(X_train, y_train)

# Fit LPM using statsmodels for detailed statistics
X_train_sm = sm.add_constant(X_train)
X_test_sm = sm.add_constant(X_test)

lpm_statsmodels = sm.OLS(y_train, X_train_sm).fit()

print("LPM Model fitted successfully")
print("LPM Coefficients (sklearn):", lpm_model.coef_)
print("LPM Intercept (sklearn):", lpm_model.intercept_)

# ============================================================================
# Model 2: Logistic Regression (sklearn)
# ============================================================================
print("\n" + "=" * 60)
print("MODEL 2: LOGISTIC REGRESSION (sklearn)")
print("=" * 60)

# Fit logistic regression
logit_sklearn = LogisticRegression(random_state=42, max_iter=1000)
logit_sklearn.fit(X_train, y_train)

print("Logistic Regression Model fitted successfully")
print("Logistic Coefficients (sklearn):", logit_sklearn.coef_[0])
print("Logistic Intercept (sklearn):", logit_sklearn.intercept_[0])

# ============================================================================
# Model 3: GLM with Binomial family and Logit link (statsmodels)
# ============================================================================
print("\n" + "=" * 60)
print("MODEL 3: GLM BINOMIAL WITH LOGIT LINK")
print("=" * 60)

# Fit GLM using statsmodels
glm_binomial = sm.GLM(y_train, X_train_sm, family=Binomial()).fit()

print("GLM Binomial Model fitted successfully")
print("GLM Coefficients:", glm_binomial.params[1:].values)  # Exclude intercept
print("GLM Intercept:", glm_binomial.params.iloc[0])

# ============================================================================
# Model 4: Logistic Regression (statsmodels) for direct comparison
# ============================================================================
print("\n" + "=" * 60)
print("MODEL 4: LOGISTIC REGRESSION (statsmodels)")
print("=" * 60)

# Fit logistic regression using statsmodels
logit_statsmodels = sm.Logit(y_train, X_train_sm).fit()

print("Statsmodels Logistic Regression fitted successfully")
print("Logistic Coefficients (statsmodels):", logit_statsmodels.params[1:].values)
print("Logistic Intercept (statsmodels):", logit_statsmodels.params.iloc[0])

# ============================================================================
# Demonstrate Equivalence: GLM vs Logistic Regression
# ============================================================================
print("\n" + "=" * 60)
print("EQUIVALENCE DEMONSTRATION")
print("=" * 60)

print("GLM Binomial coefficients:")
print(glm_binomial.params)
print("\nStatsmodels Logistic coefficients:")
print(logit_statsmodels.params)
print("\nDifference (should be ~0):")
print(glm_binomial.params - logit_statsmodels.params)
print(f"\nMaximum absolute difference: {np.max(np.abs(glm_binomial.params - logit_statsmodels.params)):.10f}")

# Verify log-likelihoods are identical
print(f"\nGLM Log-likelihood: {glm_binomial.llf:.6f}")
print(f"Logistic Log-likelihood: {logit_statsmodels.llf:.6f}")
print(f"Difference in log-likelihood: {abs(glm_binomial.llf - logit_statsmodels.llf):.10f}")

# ============================================================================
# K-NEAREST NEIGHBORS (FIXED AT K=9)
# ============================================================================
import time
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score
from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score, precision_score, recall_score, f1_score, confusion_matrix

# 1. Scaling
scaler = StandardScaler()
X_train_scaled = scaler.fit_transform(X_train)
X_test_scaled = scaler.transform(X_test)

# 2. Hardcoding K to 9 as requested
optimal_k = 9

# To keep your plot from crashing, we create data points for k values 
# around your chosen k=9 to show the "neighborhood"
k_values = range(1, 21)
cv_scores_mean = []
cv_scores_std = []

for k in k_values:
    knn_temp = KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=k)
    scores = cross_val_score(knn_temp, X_train_scaled, y_train, cv=5)
    cv_scores_mean.append(scores.mean())
    cv_scores_std.append(scores.std())

# ============================================================================
# Visualization & Final Evaluation
# ============================================================================
plt.figure(figsize=(14, 10))

# Subplot 1: K-Value Selection (Highlighting 9)
plt.subplot(2, 2, 1)
plt.errorbar(k_values, cv_scores_mean, yerr=cv_scores_std, marker='o', capsize=5)
plt.axvline(x=9, color='red', linestyle='--', label='Target k=9')
plt.xlabel('Number of Neighbors (k)')
plt.ylabel('CV Accuracy')
plt.title('KNN: Accuracy across K-values')
plt.legend()

# 3. Final Model Training (Using k=9)
final_knn = KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=9, metric='euclidean', weights='uniform')
start_time = time.time()
final_knn.fit(X_train_scaled, y_train)
train_time = time.time() - start_time

y_test_pred_knn = final_knn.predict(X_test_scaled)

# Subplot 2: Confusion Matrix
plt.subplot(2, 2, 2)
cm_knn = confusion_matrix(y_test, y_test_pred_knn)
sns.heatmap(cm_knn, annot=True, fmt='d', cmap='Blues')
plt.title(f'KNN Confusion Matrix (k=9)')
plt.xlabel('Predicted')
plt.ylabel('Actual')

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

# Final Metrics Output
print(f"--- KNN Final Report (k=9) ---")
print(f"Test Accuracy: {accuracy_score(y_test, y_test_pred_knn):.4f}")
print(f"F1-Score:      {f1_score(y_test, y_test_pred_knn):.4f}")
print(f"Training Time: {train_time:.4f}s")

# ============================================================================
# DECISION TREE IMPLEMENTATION AND ANALYSIS
# ============================================================================
print("\n" + "=" * 80)
print("DECISION TREE IMPLEMENTATION AND ANALYSIS")
print("=" * 80)

feature_names = X_train.columns.values

# ============================================================================
# Splitting Criteria Comparison
# ============================================================================
print("\n" + "=" * 60)
print("SPLITTING CRITERIA COMPARISON")
print("=" * 60)

splitting_criteria = ['gini', 'entropy']
criteria_results = {}

for criterion in splitting_criteria:
    dt = DecisionTreeClassifier(criterion=criterion, random_state=42)
    cv_scores = cross_val_score(dt, X_train, y_train, cv=5, scoring='accuracy')
    criteria_results[criterion] = {
        'mean': cv_scores.mean(),
        'std': cv_scores.std()
    }
    print(f"{criterion.capitalize():>8}: {cv_scores.mean():.4f} (+/- {cv_scores.std():.4f})")

best_criterion = max(criteria_results.keys(), key=lambda x: criteria_results[x]['mean'])
print(f"\nBest splitting criterion: {best_criterion}")

# ============================================================================
# Hyperparameter Tuning for Decision Tree
# ============================================================================
print("\n" + "=" * 60)
print("DECISION TREE HYPERPARAMETER TUNING")
print("=" * 60)

param_grid_dt = {
    'max_depth': [3, 5, 7, 10, 15, None],
    'min_samples_split': [2, 5, 10, 20],
    'min_samples_leaf': [1, 2, 5, 10],
    'criterion': [best_criterion]
}

dt_grid = GridSearchCV(
    DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=42),
    param_grid_dt,
    cv=5,
    scoring='accuracy',
    n_jobs=-1
)

print("Performing grid search for optimal hyperparameters...")
dt_grid.fit(X_train, y_train)

print(f"Best parameters: {dt_grid.best_params_}")
print(f"Best cross-validation score: {dt_grid.best_score_:.4f}")

# ============================================================================
# Tree Complexity Analysis
# ============================================================================
print("\n" + "=" * 60)
print("TREE COMPLEXITY ANALYSIS")
print("=" * 60)

max_depths = range(1, 21)
dt_train_scores = []
dt_val_scores = []

for depth in max_depths:

# Analyze how sensitive each algorithm is to hyperparameter changes
def hyperparameter_sensitivity(estimator, param_grid, X, y, cv=5):
    """Analyze sensitivity to hyperparameter changes"""
    baseline_score = cross_val_score(estimator, X, y, cv=cv).mean()
    
    sensitivities = {}
    for param, values in param_grid.items():
        param_scores = []
        for value in values:
            estimator_copy = estimator.__class__(**estimator.get_params())
            estimator_copy.set_params(**{param: value})
            score = cross_val_score(estimator_copy, X, y, cv=cv).mean()
            param_scores.append(score)
        
        # Calculate sensitivity as standard deviation of scores
        sensitivities[param] = {
            'scores': param_scores,
            'sensitivity': np.std(param_scores),
            'range': max(param_scores) - min(param_scores)
        }
    
    return sensitivities

# KNN sensitivity
knn_sensitivity_grid = {
    'n_neighbors': [3, 5, 7, 11, 15, 21],
    'weights': ['uniform', 'distance']
}

# Note: For KNN sensitivity, we'll use a simpler approach due to categorical params

for k in [3, 5, 7, 11, 15, 21]:

    score = cross_val_score(knn_temp, X_train_scaled, y_train, cv=5).mean()

# Decision Tree sensitivity

    'max_depth': [3, 5, 7, 10, 15, None],

}

dt_depth_scores = []
for depth in [3, 5, 7, 10, 15, 20]:  # Use 20 instead of None for numeric comparison
    dt_temp = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=depth, random_state=42)
    score = cross_val_score(dt_temp, X_train, y_train, cv=5).mean()
    dt_depth_scores.append(score)

print(f"KNN k-parameter sensitivity (std): {np.std(knn_k_scores):.4f}")
print(f"Decision Tree depth sensitivity (std): {np.std(dt_depth_scores):.4f}")

# Plot sensitivity analysis
axes[1, 2].plot([3, 5, 7, 11, 15, 21], knn_k_scores, 'o-', label='KNN (k)', linewidth=2)
axes[1, 2].plot([3, 5, 7, 10, 15, 20], dt_depth_scores, 'o-', label='DT (depth)', linewidth=2)

# ============================================================================
# Comprehensive Performance Metrics
# ============================================================================

def calculate_comprehensive_metrics_models(y_true, y_pred, y_prob=None):
    """Calculate comprehensive classification metrics"""
    from sklearn.metrics import (accuracy_score, precision_score, recall_score, 
                                f1_score, confusion_matrix, roc_auc_score,
                                classification_report)
    
    # Confusion matrix
    cm = confusion_matrix(y_true, y_pred)
    tn, fp, fn, tp = cm.ravel()
    
    # Basic metrics
    accuracy = accuracy_score(y_true, y_pred)
    precision = precision_score(y_true, y_pred, zero_division=0)
    recall = recall_score(y_true, y_pred, zero_division=0)
    specificity = tn / (tn + fp) if (tn + fp) > 0 else 0
    f1_metric = f1_score(y_true, y_pred, zero_division=0)
    
    # Additional metrics
    npv = tn / (tn + fn) if (tn + fn) > 0 else 0  # Negative predictive value
    
    metrics_dict = {
        'Accuracy': accuracy,
        'Precision': precision,
        'Recall': recall,
        'Specificity': specificity,
        'F1_Score': f1_metric,
        'NPV': npv,
        'TP': tp, 'TN': tn, 'FP': fp, 'FN': fn
    }
    
    # ROC AUC if probabilities provided
    if y_prob is not None:
        try:
            auc = roc_auc_score(y_true, y_prob)
            metrics_dict['ROC_AUC'] = auc
        except:
            metrics_dict['ROC_AUC'] = np.nan
    
    return metrics_dict

# Calculate metrics for both models
knn_train_metrics = calculate_comprehensive_metrics_models(y_train, y_train_pred_knn_final)
knn_test_metrics = calculate_comprehensive_metrics_models(y_test, y_test_pred_knn_final, y_test_prob_knn_final)

dt_train_metrics = calculate_comprehensive_metrics_models(y_train, y_train_pred_dt_final)
dt_test_metrics = calculate_comprehensive_metrics_models(y_test, y_test_pred_dt_final, y_test_prob_dt_final)

Model Performance Comparison and Diagnostics¶

  • Model Performance Metrics

    • Overall Performance: The Decision Tree (DT) consistently outperforms KNN across all key test set metrics, achieving higher Accuracy (approx. 0.844 vs 0.825), Precision, Recall, F1_Score, and ROC_AUC.
    • ROC Analysis: The Decision Tree demonstrates superior classification power with an AUC of 0.878, compared to 0.857 for the KNN model.
    • Accuracy Stability: Both models show consistent performance across different cross-validation strategies, including KFold and Stratified KFold, with the Decision Tree maintaining a higher accuracy range (0.84-0.85) than KNN (0.82).

  • Computational and Robustness Analysis

    • Efficiency Trade-offs: KNN has nearly zero training time but is computationally expensive during prediction (approx. 6.2 seconds), whereas the Decision Tree trains quickly and provides near-instantaneous predictions.
    • Noise Tolerance: The Decision Tree maintains high stability (approx. 0.844 accuracy) up to a noise level of 0.150, while KNN accuracy remains consistently lower and shows more fluctuation with added noise.
    • Learning Curves: Both models exhibit healthy learning patterns as validation accuracy increases with training set size, though the Decision Tree consistently reaches a higher performance ceiling.

  • High-Dimensionality and Complexity Analysis (KNN)

    • Dimensionality Curse: KNN performance peaks at low dimensions (5-10) and drops sharply as dimensionality increases toward 100, where test accuracy falls below 0.80.
    • Overfitting Trends: In high-dimensional spaces, KNN shows significant overfitting, particularly with lower k-values (k=3), where the gap between training and test accuracy exceeds 13%.
    • Distance Concentration: As dimensionality increases, the mean distance to nearest neighbors rises from approx. 0 to nearly 12, making data points less distinguishable.

  • Classification Diagnostics

    • Error Distribution: Confusion matrices reveal the Decision Tree correctly identifies more True Negatives (6,978) and True Positives (1,268) than the KNN model (6,858 and 1,214 respectively).
    • Hyperparameter Sensitivity: Validation scores for the Decision Tree peak sharply at a Max Depth of 10, while KNN performance shows a more gradual increase, stabilizing near k=30.
    • Decision Logic: Decision Tree behavior is primarily driven by financial indicators such as capital.gain (0.3386) and capital.loss (0.1504), providing a more interpretable model than the distance-based KNN approach.

print("GENERATING HIGH-DIMENSIONAL SYNTHETIC DATA")
print("=" * 60)

def generate_high_dimensional_data(n_samples=500, dimensions_list=[2, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100], n_classes=2):
    """Generate synthetic data in various dimensions"""
    np.random.seed(42)
    datasets = {}
    
    for dim in dimensions_list:
        # Generate data with some structure
        X = np.random.randn(n_samples, dim)
        
        # Create separable classes with some overlap
        # Class 1: shifted in first few dimensions
        class_1_size = n_samples // 2
        X[:class_1_size, :min(3, dim)] += 1.5
        
        # Class 2: shifted in different dimensions
        X[class_1_size:, :min(3, dim)] -= 1.5
        
        y = np.hstack([np.zeros(class_1_size), np.ones(n_samples - class_1_size)])
        
        datasets[dim] = (X, y)
        print(f"Generated {dim}D dataset: {X.shape}, classes: {np.bincount(y.astype(int))}")
    
    return datasets

datasets = generate_high_dimensional_data()

# ============================================================================
# Distance Concentration Analysis
# ============================================================================
print("\n" + "=" * 60)
print("DISTANCE CONCENTRATION ANALYSIS")
print("=" * 60)

def analyze_distance_concentration(datasets):
    """Analyze how distances concentrate in high dimensions"""
    results = {}
    
    for dim, (X, y) in datasets.items():
        # Calculate pairwise distances
        distances = pdist(X[:100], metric='euclidean')  # Use subset for efficiency
        
        # Statistics
        min_dist = np.min(distances)
        max_dist = np.max(distances)
        mean_dist = np.mean(distances)
        std_dist = np.std(distances)
        
        # Distance concentration ratio
        concentration_ratio = (max_dist - min_dist) / min_dist
        
        results[dim] = {
            'min_dist': min_dist,
            'max_dist': max_dist,
            'mean_dist': mean_dist,
            'std_dist': std_dist,
            'concentration_ratio': concentration_ratio,
            'distances': distances
        }
        
        print(f"Dimension {dim:3d}: min={min_dist:.3f}, max={max_dist:.3f}, "
              f"ratio={concentration_ratio:.3f}, cv={std_dist/mean_dist:.3f}")
    
    return results

distance_results = analyze_distance_concentration(datasets)

# KNN Performance vs Dimensionality
# ============================================================================
print("\n" + "=" * 60)

print("=" * 60)

def evaluate_knn_performance_by_dimension(datasets, k_values=[3, 5, 7]):
    """Evaluate KNN performance across dimensions"""
    performance_results = {}
    
    for dim, (X, y) in datasets.items():
        # Split data
        X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.3, random_state=42)
        
        # Scale features
        scaler = StandardScaler()
        X_train_scaled = scaler.fit_transform(X_train)
        X_test_scaled = scaler.transform(X_test)
        
        dim_results = {}
        for k in k_values:
            # Train KNN
            knn = KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=k)
            knn.fit(X_train_scaled, y_train)
            
            # Evaluate
            train_acc = knn.score(X_train_scaled, y_train)
            test_acc = knn.score(X_test_scaled, y_test)
            
            dim_results[k] = {
                'train_accuracy': train_acc,
                'test_accuracy': test_acc,
                'overfitting': train_acc - test_acc
            }
        
        performance_results[dim] = dim_results
        print(f"Dimension {dim:3d}: Test Acc k=3: {dim_results[3]['test_accuracy']:.3f}, "
              f"k=5: {dim_results[5]['test_accuracy']:.3f}, k=7: {dim_results[7]['test_accuracy']:.3f}")
    
    return performance_results

knn_performance = evaluate_knn_performance_by_dimension(datasets)

# ============================================================================
# Nearest Neighbor Distance Analysis
# ============================================================================
print("\n" + "=" * 60)
print("NEAREST NEIGHBOR DISTANCE ANALYSIS")
print("=" * 60)

def analyze_nearest_neighbor_distances(datasets, n_neighbors=5):
    """Analyze how nearest neighbor distances change with dimension"""
    nn_results = {}
    
    for dim, (X, y) in datasets.items():
        # Scale features
        scaler = StandardScaler()
        X_scaled = scaler.fit_transform(X)
        
        # Calculate nearest neighbor distances
        knn_model = KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=n_neighbors + 1)  # +1 to exclude self
        knn_model.fit(X_scaled, y)
        
        # Get distances to nearest neighbors
        distances, indices = knn_model.kneighbors(X_scaled[:100])  # Use subset for efficiency
        
        # Remove distance to self (first column)
        nn_distances = distances[:, 1:]
        
        # Statistics
        mean_nn_dist = np.mean(nn_distances)
        std_nn_dist = np.std(nn_distances)
        min_nn_dist = np.mean(np.min(nn_distances, axis=1))
        max_nn_dist = np.mean(np.max(nn_distances, axis=1))
        
        nn_results[dim] = {
            'mean_nn_distance': mean_nn_dist,
            'std_nn_distance': std_nn_dist,
            'min_nn_distance': min_nn_dist,
            'max_nn_distance': max_nn_dist,
            'nn_distances': nn_distances
        }
        
        print(f"Dimension {dim:3d}: Mean NN dist={mean_nn_dist:.3f}, "
              f"Std={std_nn_dist:.3f}, CV={std_nn_dist/mean_nn_dist:.3f}")
    
    return nn_results

for k in [3, 5, 7]:
    overfitting = [knn_performance[dim][k]['overfitting'] for dim in dimensions]
    axes[1, 1].semilogx(dimensions, overfitting, 'o-', label=f'k={k}', linewidth=2, markersize=6)

axes[1, 1].set_xlabel('Number of Dimensions')
axes[1, 1].set_ylabel('Overfitting (Train Acc - Test Acc)')
axes[1, 1].set_title('KNN Overfitting vs Dimensionality')
axes[1, 1].legend()
axes[1, 1].grid(True, alpha=0.3)

# 6. Coefficient of variation of distances
cv_distances = [distance_results[dim]['std_dist'] / distance_results[dim]['mean_dist'] 
               for dim in dimensions]

axes[1, 2].semilogx(dimensions, cv_distances, 'o-', linewidth=2, markersize=8, color='purple')
axes[1, 2].set_xlabel('Number of Dimensions')
axes[1, 2].set_ylabel('Coefficient of Variation\n(std/mean)')
axes[1, 2].set_title('Distance Variability vs Dimensionality')
axes[1, 2].grid(True, alpha=0.3)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
from sklearn.feature_selection import SelectKBest, f_classif

# Test PCA dimensionality reduction
print("DIMENSIONALITY REDUCTION WITH PCA:")

high_dim_data = datasets[50]  # Use 50D data
X_high, y_high = high_dim_data

# Split data
X_train_high, X_test_high, y_train_high, y_test_high = train_test_split(
    X_high, y_high, test_size=0.3, random_state=42)

# Scale data
scaler = StandardScaler()
X_train_scaled_high = scaler.fit_transform(X_train_high)
X_test_scaled_high = scaler.transform(X_test_high)

# Test different numbers of PCA components
pca_components = [2, 5, 10, 20, 30]
pca_results = {}

for n_comp in pca_components:
    # Apply PCA
    pca = PCA(n_components=n_comp, random_state=42)
    X_train_pca = pca.fit_transform(X_train_scaled_high)
    X_test_pca = pca.transform(X_test_scaled_high)
    
    # Train KNN on reduced data
    knn_pca = KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=5)
    knn_pca.fit(X_train_pca, y_train_high)
    
    # Evaluate
    test_acc = knn_pca.score(X_test_pca, y_test_high)
    explained_var = np.sum(pca.explained_variance_ratio_)
    
    pca_results[n_comp] = {
        'accuracy': test_acc,
        'explained_variance': explained_var
    }
    
    print(f"  PCA {n_comp:2d} components: Accuracy={test_acc:.4f}, "
          f"Explained Var={explained_var:.4f}")

# Baseline (no dimensionality reduction)
knn_baseline = KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=5)
knn_baseline.fit(X_train_scaled_high, y_train_high)
baseline_acc = knn_baseline.score(X_test_scaled_high, y_test_high)
print(f"  No reduction (50D): Accuracy={baseline_acc:.4f}")

print(f"\nCONCLUSION:")
best_pca_comp = max(pca_results.keys(), key=lambda x: pca_results[x]['accuracy'])
best_pca_acc = pca_results[best_pca_comp]['accuracy']

if best_pca_acc > baseline_acc:
    print(f"  PCA improved performance: {best_pca_acc:.4f} vs {baseline_acc:.4f}")
    print(f"  Best: {best_pca_comp} components explaining "
          f"{pca_results[best_pca_comp]['explained_variance']:.1%} of variance")
else:
    print(f"  PCA did not improve performance in this case")
    print(f"  This demonstrates that curse of dimensionality effects vary by dataset")

FINAL VERDICT¶

Model Selection: Logistic/GLM (SM)¶

Based on the provided test performance summary, the Logistic/GLM (SM) model is the optimal choice for this binomial dataset.

1. Primary Metric: F1-Score¶

The F1-Score is the harmonic mean of Precision and Recall, making it the most reliable metric for binomial data where you need a balance between "finding all positives" and "being correct when you do."

  • Logistic/GLM (SM): 0.6407 (Highest)
  • Logistic (Sklearn): 0.6328
  • Decision Tree: 0.6248

The GLM (SM) successfully optimizes the trade-off, achieving the highest Recall (0.5710) without significantly compromising Precision.

2. Probabilistic Accuracy (Brier Score)¶

In binomial classification, the Brier Score measures the accuracy of predicted probabilities (how close the prediction is to the actual 0 or 1 outcome).

  • Logistic/GLM (SM): 0.1090 (Lowest/Best)
  • Logistic (Sklearn): 0.1107
  • LPM (OLS): 0.1204

The lower Brier score indicates that this model is better calibrated and provides more "trustworthy" probability estimates than the other candidates.

3. Discriminatory Power (ROC-AUC)¶

The ROC-AUC represents the model's ability to distinguish between classes across all possible thresholds.

  • Logistic/GLM (SM): 0.8869 (Highest)

This suggests that even if you were to change the classification threshold (e.g., from 0.5 to 0.3) to capture more positive cases, the Logistic/GLM would still maintain the best separation between your two groups.

4. Comparison with Other Models¶

  • LPM (OLS): While computationally simple, the Linear Probability Model is mathematically ill-suited for binomial data. It produced the lowest Recall (0.4639) and F1-score, likely due to predicting values outside the [0, 1] range.
  • KNN & Decision Tree: These non-parametric models struggled to match the predictive power of the Logistic regressions, particularly in Recall, suggesting the underlying data likely follows a logistic distribution.

Conclusion: The Logistic/GLM (SM) is the most robust and accurate model across all key performance indicators.
